entries.text: Part I.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: January 13, 1990: Berry Creek Tour

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: A.  Smith Hill Wildlife

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you mind giving us your memories of them right now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, if I can remember anything that I can tell you about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Right now we're near stop 2 [of the Soap Creek Auto Tour], we're looking to the due east on what is called Smith Hill now and with James Hanish. And Jim, could you tell me what this hill used to be called, as you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It used to be called, as I remember, Polks Hill, P-o-l-k-s, named after the family that had that farmland there [family of Bert Folks]. And on top there was . . . thought there was rattlesnakes but only at the extreme top. But I never hunted up there, but that was sort of a valley landmark.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall when any. . . who told you that there rattlesnakes there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Local neighbors. It was not advisory to go up there in the hot summer like August or September.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any other types of wildlife that. . . was there any talk of wolves or bears?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or opossums or anything else associated with this hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we didn't have opossums in here at that time, we had mostly some fox, and no bears or wolves. And occasionally, once in a while, a wild cat, but they were very scarce. But mostly it . . . most of the animal life was deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the foxes, were those grey foxes or red foxes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They reported caught and trapped is a red fox. They were mostly found out in the extreme valley because the wildlife like young pheasants and chickens and stuff would belong to ranchers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall when the red foxes were being trapped, what years?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, in the '30's, as far as I can remember back. And there wasn't any mink or beaver here at that time in any of these creeks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No beaver at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was no sign of any beaver.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now I hear that the red fox was brought in, the first one being trapped on Soap Creek side was 1938. Do you think the red fox were native or do you think they were brought in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really couldn't tell you on that part. Like I say where we live we didn't have too we stayed within our environmental or our boundaries of where we lived and we didn't get too much information that went on in other areas of the valley except what we read in the newspaper.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So on Polk Hill, that would have just been word of mouth, you wouldn't have.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Word of mouth, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did the Folks live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lived in a house at the base of that hill, on the north side at the base of the hill. Of course, those days when somebody lived on a property it was a hill or particular landmark they called it the name of the people that lived there. So maybe through the county maps or the state they wouldn't be actively named.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall anything else about this hill right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not a thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kevin do you have a question about here on the Indians?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Do you recall anything in reference to the Indians in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The only thing that I heard was . . . what I found was like an arrowheads and I have some small burred arrowheads but they're down in Klamath Falls. They were found in the flats along Berry Creek on the Dickey property.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, we will be going down there at that point we can talk about them. Do you recall any talk about the Indians up on any of these peaks or ridges?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was nothing said about the Indians that lived up there, they probably hunted and come through, but along Berry Creek, there was considerable Indian mortar. grinding bowls found and pestles out of stone. Now the strange thing, this rock in here is what we used to call the iron rock, it's got a rusty outward appearance, if you hit it, it chips off. But the Indian bowls were made out of a big, smooth rock, like they might have gotten out of a river, maybe they brought them up from the Willamette or the Calapooia River.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they weren't native rock?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not to here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall anything other than stories about rattlesnakes about this particular area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not a thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's all you equated it with, that there were rattlesnakes up on the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's all there was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever see one, did anybody ever bring.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never did see one, and nobody ever showed me one they killed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Out at Eugene, Skinner's Butte, there's some rattlesnakes up there. And they're on the high elevations here in the valley, they won't get downwards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall what kind of rattlesnakes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not any particular name. . . they weren't called a diamond back or the other kinds of rattlesnakes just a rattlesnake.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: B.  Gardner Home

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're up on. . . I've got the recorder on again here. We're up by the tree farm sign [Smith Hill Properties] on the gate on the top of the hill, can you remember anything about the family that lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, the husband worked at the Coote's sawmill, wife didn't work and they had a boarder that stayed with them, a young man. He worked at the mill and they had two daughters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the boarder's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I really don't. It's been so long ago, but before we left, left this area, the Gardner family moved up to the Portland area and that's the last we heard of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody move into their house after they left?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this called the Gardner house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gardner family, yeah, they lived there. It was not particular house, just where the Gardners lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Gardner place maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this apple orchard that's in here would have been their apple orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, . . . remember they used the food from the trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall where their house was located from this point?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wasn't too far back. It was about right around where that oak tree is, you could see it from the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have a barn or any out buildings?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they had a barn because they had a cow. And he worked the mill and his wife used to milk the cow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall about how many acres they might have had in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really don't know. It might have been maybe they didn't own the land, but see here in this territory there was farm houses and things and it might have been just pay so much rent maybe the land owner . . . they might have paid rent to Joe Smith for all we know. They never said. But Joe Smith owned a lot of land in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So John Smith was his son?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And inherited the land from Joe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know. I don't think. . . I couldn't tell you whether he had any other children or not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any other houses in this area up here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No this is the only house that I recall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know the names of the men that the daughters married?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, Lord no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You didn't know them very well?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't know . . . the girls I didn't know very well. Because like I say, they moved away before they got married here, they moved up to Portland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall what year that was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I really couldn't tell you. It was . . . no, long before the war, long before the war.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall if anybody else moved into this house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, 'cause see, when . . . after, they left shortly after we left and I didn't know . we didn't come back here anymore. I don't know if anybody else did move in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, we might as well. . . can you recall what year you moved in here, into this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I talked to my mother about it, and she . . . we lost the records and she thought it

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: might have been somewhere . . . get there and went into in '33, '34 . . . it was the early twenties I would say.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you moved out in '33 or '34?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can give you a pretty good idea. I'm 78 now, and I was about 17 or 18 years old when we moved up here, so subtract that from

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sixty years ago.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About sixty years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would be 1930?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In that period.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did you move from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we moved from Sunnyside, California, up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So is that first your family ever came to Oregon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, the first. We had ten acres of young orange trees planted down there in Sunnyside and some chickens, we had around . . . . five hundred chickens and we decided to move to Oregon where we contacted different real estate people and we found this man by the name of Anderson. He had this homestead up here. So we traded even Steven for the homestead.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He moved down to Sunnyside and you moved up to Anderson's homestead?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yeah, he was a real estate man as far as I could remember. He just bought our property as a something to invest in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. So this was maybe a holding he had here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he had this hundred and sixty acres holding. So we moved up here and then we . . . we couldn't live on hundred and sixty acres, it was too wild, there was no house no nothing. He contacted Joe Smith and he found us forty acres out here. At that time Judge McHenry of Corvallis, his son . . . Judge McHenry now . . . the McHenry now that had the funeral parlor, his father. . . the old Judge McHenry, at one time he was district attorney and he was the one that closed the deal for us with this Joe Smith family. . . . We've known Judge McHenry and Joseph McHenry. In fact, I joined the American Legion when Joe was one of our members.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you got the hundred and sixty acres where was that located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was located . . . all right . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was located . . . like from the Coote's sawmill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If it's down here, we can probably talk about that when we get down here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we'll do that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'll put it on my notes here then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything else about the Gardners here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember the vegetation up here, what did it look like when the Gardner's lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just like this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Looked just about the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No change.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's what everybody's been telling me, this is just about the way it looked in the 1920's and '30's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, this country hasn't changed one bit, the trees haven't grown . . . a hell of a lot, some of the old orchards are still alive, but they're about dead, but. . . the tarp, what you want to call the flora of this place is the same.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The. . . was there any logging going on up in here at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There might have been, I'm not sure how. . . I think Mr. Coote, he logged. . . but he probably did log in here. He logged along the lower part of the creek. See, that creek came down out of the mountain, I think you called it Savage Creek. It comes down . . . it flows between Polks Peak and the plateau. The hundred and sixty acres was located on the plateau.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we'll be going into that area there so as we get there we can look at it. . . look at the fog and then talk about it in more detail there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you. . . nothing else about this area? Looks the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not a thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One more thing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's lots of skunks and yellow jackets, and wasps and hornets in this country.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Through the whole country, or just up here on the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just generally.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you call them civet cats or skunks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They're regular . . . I would call just plain skunks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yellow jackets, wasps, and skunks through the whole area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: C.  Coote's Mill

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right at the base of the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're down at the base of a hill looking at the Coote's sawmill site, we'll be going to the right here. Where did the Polks live from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lived back, the house was back there about a mile and half at the base of the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the old Greenberiy Smith homestead, did anybody call that anything by the donation land claims at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that was just always a farm, it was always here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so it was the Polks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they have anything to do with the. . no, Polk County was named after.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From the Polks to this road here, were there any other families living along this hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so, as far as I can remember there were no families on this side at all. Except down maybe by the Berry Creek Bridge there was a family but their land didn't extend this far.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So was this Polk's land all the way up to here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I really couldn't tell you that much, but I know that the Polks lived over there and we . . . I know there used to be cattle grazing out here and I thought it maybe belonged to the Polks family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there's cattle grazing out through here, what's this landscape look like compared to then, have you noticed any general changes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not a change.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's all pretty similar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, to me it looks alike, but every time I come out here gradually, I haven't seen any changes at all. Except that there's a little more scrub growth coming out into the fields than there was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now these apple trees down off on the right here, was that part of an orchard that was existing at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because all through this country there's.. . . you'll find even up in the wilderness area you'll find apple, small apple orchards, they were planted by the pioneers and then they had a homestead and then they left and the orchard bloomed and the deer ate the fruit and the seeds dropped through out the forest and young trees would start.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think the wildings were moved by deer more than say birds or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, maybe either one but I would think. . . both bird and deer would have something to say about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This little orchard in here, do you think this was planted or do you think it was a wild orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wouldn't think it would be planted because why would they plant so far from the house, because the house like you say was way over there. I think they're seeds that blown, just like the old Johnny Appleseed theory.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was the school that was in this area here, was it pretty close to us?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, pretty close, right down almost in this flat. Now we see there's some little colored stuff over there, the school was right there and it was . . . I believe they used to use it . . . the district used it for a church on Sunday, too. There's also a church in Airlie but the school was right down in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About where those beehives are?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I don't know if there's any remnants of the school or not, but that's just the area it was in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Berry Creek School House.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was called the Berry Creek School House here, about where the bee hives are?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, this is the Berry Creek District from the base of this hill all encompassing this

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And it was used as church, what denomination?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, any denomination.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So kind of all people just gathered here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they had it . . . like any service, you didn't have Catholic or anything, you just had a chaplain and that was it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So did you ever go to this church?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know any of the families that did?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the Cootes went, he was the owner of the sawmill, and I don't think Burkes went, and Dodgson, they used to go to Airlie, they had a Baptist Church of some kind of a church in Airlie, they went to that one. And I don't think Gardners, Gardners might have sent their kids to Sunday School here but. . . we didn't call it church out here, we belonged to churches back east, I was born and raised in Chicago. But we didn't go to church out here, worked all week in the woods and the Sunday I'd go fishing or go out with boys and have some beer. That was it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was more Jim to go out and have a beer than go listen to a sermon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Now we belong to the Presbyterian Church in Corvallis, we go to that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the left we're looking at the road as it comes in now and we're looking at some plastic covering on hay, can you tell me about where the Coote's sawmill was in relation to what we're seeing to the west here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If we could

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We can drive down this road, would that be better?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, if we can get there then I can . . . we can find possibly, there must be something left of the mill road and creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So if we take this road out here can we follow it out pretty far with out getting disoriented or should we come back to this later?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think you'll. . . it's only . . . you can get up there a ways, I think you were here once before and there was a fence there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was the next road down. . . no, we. . . we did come in here, but now we've got a key [to the fence today so we're not stopped. Should we. . . do you want to head off in this

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: direction now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, let's go up in here and see if we can find the sawmill, that's where it would be up in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we're looking at the cows, could you comment on what the cattle were like as you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, when I lived here there were mostly dairy cattle and I thought one time that I would maybe start raising some beef but I could not buy a Hereford calf in this [Willamette] valley. You could airy but I wanted young herefords to start to the herd, so when I went down to Southern California working and after about five or six years I came back and the valley was full of herefords.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you. . . . about '33 or '34, before you left, there weren't any herefords that you could locate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I couldn't find a hereford calf at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you came back, say, right before World War II, then the whole. . . everybody had changed over to herefords?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, a lot of people changed over to herefords.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's what we're looking at here now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is a type of domestic animal that came in during the 1930's during the Depression?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Evidently in here because, see at one time people wouldn't even bother raising a calf, it cost too much so they would kill, and that's one reason there was a scarcity of calves.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And probably an abundance of veal?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's what caused the scarcity of veal too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so this is all dairy farms where people had cows?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. . . . no, this wasn't all dairy but they had a mixed breed, the people that had cows they didn't have any big herds in here at all. People that lived over there had maybe two or three cows for milking. We had a cow, when we lived up there. Dickeys had a couple cows, maybe three or four. Everybody had a cow that lived here, but their cows were either Jerseys, they were the best milk givers, or Hoisteins. There wasn't what they call the regular beef blood in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did people use for beef, just old dairy cows, worn out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No they'd take a calf regardless of it's breed and have it castrated and kill it later on for beef.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so they'd raise beef but it wouldn't. . . mostly the off-shoot of the dairy herds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And then for other meat they raised hogs, there was a lot of sheep in here at one time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the sheep raised for meat or wool?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they raised them in shares. We raised some sheep, we raised about thirty sheep on shares with a landowner. We'd take care of the sheep and when he'd go to sell them, we'd get half of the price of wool brought in or meat weight in the lambs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was actually a dual crop, both sheared and meat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This area that we're in right here, this was the mill site though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's a mill site and I believe it was up further.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we'll just drive up there then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're about where the sawmill site was.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was about right up in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About right at this second gate here, or was it maybe a little bit further along?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well there was a creek. . . where in the hell that there creek was . . . it wouldn't have been in this district, it would have been up further but it was on the creek that come out between the hills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the mill was right along the creek edge here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any other buildings?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was houses that the sawmill families lived in, there were right over in that district there on that flat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Over on that flat to our east from this road, maybe where that little strip of. . . looks like oak and fir.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And some were over there and some were along the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Some houses along the creek here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you draw that on . . . my page here so I can keep it? [Map in Research Forests file]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see now,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you want me to leave you alone there to draw for awhile, or do you want me to.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, now there's the peak and that country there . . . approaches it where

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you call that Forest Peak right up in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it's further up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, it's the next one over to the west.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When we come around that hump that's where we come around, all that country over there. It's a hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay and that hill is definitely Polk Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All right, now the creek runs up into here

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We'll be driving up there in a little bit here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this here is a fairly easy slope, but you get up here and it's a deep canyon. You don't want that. But on this side about in here was our hundred and sixty acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's where our timber was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And we should be driving through that pretty quick.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, let's see, now the road came down . . . the hill was about like that and and this creek comes down and they built a bridge like this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We'll want to try and locate the bridge when we get up there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this road, the creek was on the right hand side by the road going up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you call that creek at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we called it that time, the south fork of Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: South Fork.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Like I said at that time everything was kind of nicknamed, there was no accuracy to it. We called it the south fork of Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said something before about the left hand and the right hand Berry Creek or. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, down below . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we'll. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where we lived, there was a creek come through there and that was the main Berry Creek and there's one that came out of here from nowhere was very small, we called that another branch of the dam creek. But this creek down here. . . the bridge down here where the Coote's house is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One was the left hand and one was the right hand?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Keep going up that way there's one to the left and this went up and disappeared in the hills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. So at this point here at the Coote's sawmill, what kind of timber did they cut?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They cut red fir, if they could find the largest trees, they handled some old growth and he had what they call a gyppo sawmill, very small and had a threshing machine engine to run it for steam for everything and it usually broke down once and a while. And they need . . couple of trucks, three or four men in the mill and two or three fallers and buckers and that was it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they get the logs to the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They . . . what they called skidded them down with horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is all horse logging?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they float any down the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. They couldn't, the creek wasn't that deep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No splash dams?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No splash dams.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any oxen or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, regular horses. Draft horses we'd used for the logging.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they brought them right to the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right, they'd skid them to the mill, yeah. Or some of them they would what they called made a plank road up into the road and then the trucker would go up there and then they would have a loading platform. The horses would skid them down and they roll them out on the truck.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be true for this mill here that they had plank roads going from this hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they had plank roads, in fact, I remember during the Depression, the men used to put in the plank road, they wanted to keep working because they had to reach more

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: timber and they could get the trucks up to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of trucks did they use?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Regular logging trucks like we have today.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Like today?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Rubber tire?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Tires, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have any tram roads through this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were up in the woods.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The tram roads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What we call the plank roads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They're made out of plank.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay and they were rubber tired vehicles driving over the plank roads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the horses would then skid down to the trucks, the loading platform?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, like here's a bank.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they build that bank or the loading platform, would that be constructed or would they take a natural bank?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They would. . . sometimes they would take and gouge it away and make the bank.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would they gouge it away? Did they have any cats or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They'd bring a Fresno up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's a Fresno?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I got you! [Laughs]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fresno are shaped like this, out of steel, and it has a long handle with a rope on it and it's kind of like a wheel or a skid and you . . . of course your horse. . . your harness and everything is at your horses ear and you just hold back on that and then you push forward to get the dirt and then when you want to dump you just push it forward and pull it back it just dumps it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So these loading platforms were built by horse labor using a tool called a Fresno.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fresno or whatever, sometimes they . . . men would have to get in and use a pick and shovel too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And hand constructed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hand constructed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the breed of draft horse they use, Belgians or Clydesdales or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No they were just far as I can remember just a general sturdy farm horse that would be used for plowing. Take it this way, one man . . . well like Gardner, he would use his horse to plow his land, his team and then he would come down and work and he'd skid logs for the mill. Like Mr. Tandy lived down there by Berry Creek. He /worked here too. And he had his team, they were big, heavy horses, but they were of the Clydesdale breed or no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just run of the mill work horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And in them days they used horses completely for plowing, well, not completely, but they had to be a good strong animal.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this area up here that we're looking at, was there any kind of crop or anything, or was this just a log yard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, some of maybe the people that lived around here might have little truck gardens, like lettuce and tomatoes and upgrade their food.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall the names of any of the families that lived in through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Only one, that was the Buttecaufs, but I don't know what ever happened to them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Buttecaufs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have any children?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they had a couple girls. Like I said, there were four or five families that lived in here and they worked here and in them days everybody was friendly to an extent but it was always somebody that wasn't too friendly with. There was always something had a squabble over something. So you didn't have a fight with them just kind of purposely avoid them. That's the way it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was kind of like a little community that kind of stuck to itself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did these people live here a long time or did they kind of move in and out with the mill flow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They moved in and out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so kind of a transitory work force?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Because . . . like lots of times in the winter you . . . he couldn't operate all year round. He couldn't get the logs in the snow, at one time there was three feet of snow in this country, you couldn't do anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall what year there was three feet of snow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My folks know, I was in California at the time. And they wrote and told me they couldn't. . . in fact the ranchers had to go out and chop down fir trees for the sheep to eat the needles, there was no feed. It was just covered.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they feed the cows, just hay that they had put up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lost a lot of cows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A bad winter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They'd have to take the hay out of the barn and scatter it out somewhere, a lot of the sheep were lost because they got buried. It showed how quickly how much it snowed. My mother said my father shoveled a path out to the barn, our barn was about hundred and fifty feet away from the house, by the time he got there, there was three inches of snow in that path. So he had to practically work all night to keep the roof from caving in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You moved here about 1930?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Somewhere in there, but it's very vague.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you were down in California maybe in the mid-30's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I went down and went to work.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And how long did your folks live here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they must. . . we must have with our timber holdings and everything, we must have lived out here, I came back to help them, I would say at least ten or twelve years or more.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Until Camp Adair came in, did they live here until Camp Adair was formed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We moved out before Camp Adair came in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was sometime, the bad snow was sometime in the mid-30's maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, because we left when Hitler started to move into provinces of. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Of where?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hitler took over Czechoslovakia.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I know I came back and I helped my folks get some pulp wood down out of the hills and then there was a headline that Hitler had taken over Czechoslovakia. And I worked here for awhile and then we disposed of the property and moved in to Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever work for Coote?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, yeah. I wanted some lumber, we'd work and take it out in lumber instead of pay. Like if we needed some two by fours or something, we'd work it out, my dad and I worked it out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so it was mostly barter.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Barter work, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of work would you do in the mill, yourself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we straightened out stuff on the, pulling green chain, straighten out the boards as they come out with a chain, maybe they'd fly all over the place and take a pick and drag them around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would he be the main employer in this area then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In this area, and that type of work, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was kind. . . some economic stability here during the depression?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, well, we were employers, we had . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see we're talking about.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We were talking about employers. Well, we

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hundred and sixty acres.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We employed people, we had a contract for the pulp and paper mill in Salem, Oregon. I don't know how many thousand feet of bulk paper, we had to cut for them. But there's a flat up there on the. . . we'd employ on an average thirty to forty people to cut and peel and stack wood for us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Thirty or forty people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would they come from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They'd come from everywhere, they were some of them school teachers, they were

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: out of work during the depression. We had a little camp up there made for them and then they would go up there and work and get grocery money and a little cash.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when we get up there maybe you can show me that camp site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's gone. It's completely, you wouldn't recognize it, it's just like this now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But could you find the area, the camping area, I mean the site or location?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think we're going to get up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. When we get close to it, let's talk about that some more.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It might not, some of this stuff you might have to scratch out but we may not have thirty or forty people but I would say we had at least fifteen or twenty because we had to get that wood out. When you take out a contract we have a deadline and like fir, the bark don't slip until around early spring. It tightens up and you can't ship it because they won't accept it with the bark on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, what was the product they were making out of the white fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Paper, paper products.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You had to be able to peel those logs and so these people were mostly peeling rather than logging?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we'd . . . we had . . . we contracted with a man to go up there with what they call a drag saw and he cut and the peelers would follow him and peel and split and pile. And see white fir was a such a heavy percent of water that lots of times that you would have to put four more inches of white fir split wood on top of a cord so the mill would get their full measure, because it shrinks. And then we had some logs, of course now, the logs had to wait, they couldn't be shipped down the river until they dried because they'd go right to the bottom.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you mean by logs, red fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: White fir logs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the white fir logs. And when you say red fir, what does that mean?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that was mostly fire wood, we cut up old growth for fire wood and made shakes out of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Out of the old growth?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was the red fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there much old growth in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we had some nice old growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they in solid stands?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Scattered.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Scattered.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Scattered stands. Well, in them days we worked by hand and it would take us two and a half hours to fall a tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A single tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A single tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now were they in. . . how big were the stands, how many trees would be in a stand?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well there wouldn't be . . . they would be isolated. One here, and maybe one over there about eighty to hundred feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So maybe three or four trees per acre?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, nothing like. . . about like that, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just three or four old growth per acre?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now were there any old oak scattered in among the old fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the oaks were there first and they'd died off because the firs grew up and shut off the sun. You had to be very careful in working in there because you'd go up to a tree that looked like a small oak tree and you could tell it was dead because the bark would be off of it and you could push it right over, because the firs, they reach for the sun right away and the oaks lost out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever count the rings on any of those old fir, any idea how old they were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we did one time, we found one that I would say was around two hundred.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About two hundred?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the stumps after the tree was fallen, the stumps would measure maybe thirty-six inches across.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So what you called old growth were about three foot, maybe /wo hundred years old.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And was that. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the bark was thick, it was about that thick.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the bark was about four inches. . . three inches.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Four inches thick.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the trees real limby, like growing so wide apart?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there wasn't any limbs, in fact if they were limbs down low we wouldn't cut them because you couldn't get nothing out of them. They'd be all knots. We had to have at least oh, say, sixty or eighty feet or more of clear lumber before we'd fall those trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would make that lumber clear, just growing up through the oak, would that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But they'd be about sixty or eighty foot clear and then they'd get limby?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they'd get limby.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Even though they were growing far apart?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there second growth in among the old growth?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was second growth among the old growths.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those would maybe seeded then from the older trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because we used to call the older trees, the grandfather trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those would be the grandfathers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the grandfathers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the younger trees, what would you call them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, just the kids.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The kids. And then the kids would go to the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the kids would go to the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the old growth would be the shingles and fire wood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, unless maybe. . . some of these small . . . what they called gyppo outfits they would handle an old growth log. And at that time we tried to sell our good lumber logs in Corvallis but they didn't want to stump it . . . they didn't want to pay any stumpage.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the prices?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know but it was fairly low. We got $4 a cord for firewood delivered to

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Salem. That had to be cut, split, . . . I mean cut, sawed, peeled, split and piled and hauled to Salem, four dollars a cord.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you had to transport it too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the white fir. . . did that grow separate from the Doug fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. That was separate.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of areas did these trees grow in, what kind of. . . were they north facing slopes or was it everywhere through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What ever, just everywhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was solid fir stand up through this country?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about these hills looking at what they call Smith Peak now and this slope here were those pretty much covered with second growth the way they are now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were just about. . . yeah, they called it second growth and like I say, some of the areas the trees advanced. There used to be more clearing than what there is. But the forest, they gradually seed and taken it over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about yew wood or other trees, were there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we had some yew wood on our place, in fact, one year there was a man that come from Pomona, California, he bought some bow stays made out of yew wood. So we took him up to the place to the hundred and sixty acres and showed him and that's a waste of a tree. You just cut . . . you have to clear say six or eight feet of trunk and the rest is limbs. You cut the tree down and then the top you can't use. But he bought, oh, I would say about fifty dollars worth of bow stay material, it makes beautiful bow stays for archery.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But it's got to be perfect, it can't have a lot pin knots in it, because that would make it weak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any oak for firewood or chittum for bark or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, there used to be people come up, we never bothered the chittum, but there was some people come up and peel chitum. They'd take it and after if dried someplace, get some money for it. Oak, we didn't have any oak, well, we had oak on the forty

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and we'd cut that and use it for our fire wood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this road here that came into the mill, did it go . . . extend further back into the logging road system, is that kind of how it went?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the road that went into the mill like I say . . . mill to here, it went back up into here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your hundred and sixty acres just started back here a short ways?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I would say it was a mile or so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Back here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up that creek. And on this slope, that's the slope we had to get up there. In fact the truck had a hell of a time getting up there. Right in here [referring to map] is where I found that spearhead.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so we're going to be heading back into the. . . so from this mill that's right here going back towards your hundred and sixty acres, there are no more buildings back up in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now did this road follow along the base of the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That we would have to find out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You can't recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know if it's still there or not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I mean, did it go along the base of this hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On this side of the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the creek. . . going up take the road to go up towards this hundred and sixty, the creek was on the right hand side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This creek here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the creek would be on the right hand side when we're heading up and then would the bridge cross the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was . . . we had a bridge across the creek up at the base of the hill. Then the creek went to the left and the bridge was built was like this and the creek went like that. And this is a canyon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're going to try to get around. . . back around there on the road here pretty quick. On this road over here on the main, what they call the Tampico Road now, was that the same alignment at that time as it is now, did that. . . ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That road where Gardners lived and everything?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Hasn't changed a bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about. . . see how that bank is filled in and all that fill is through there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that was changed, that is a change, yes. That used to be a very steep and hard thing to get up, but they did fix that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the old road

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the old site though, that's where the road was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They built it pretty much. . . they just put the fill in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know when they did that, maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really couldn't tell you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the alignment's still the same, they just improved it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To reduce the slope.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From here the school house would be over in front of us towards the east out through there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. To the left.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that the school you went to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't go to that school. I was out of school when we came out here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And then the creek going down through there, that vegetation, does that look just about the same as it used to be?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This creek here runs all the way down through and it crossed that road that we come in that time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. We'll be going that way this time just kind of intersecting. Before we leave this area is there . . . we've mentioned the mill, the houses, the families that moved in and out, and is the reason you remember that one family's name because of the daughters?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Buttecaufs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a particular reason you remember them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it probably was the name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they live here more than the other families maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say they lived here as long as the other families.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay this would be the Coote's mill site. The mill was probably here. And these hills had about the same kind of vegetation and everything is pretty similar except for the lack of buildings now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kevin you mentioned the fill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Up at the base of the hill underneath what looks like an apple tree, there's a mound of fill dirt, but I was noticing out here to the west, my question would be do you recall any impact that the soldiers had when Adair was in here in terms of maybe fox holes and maneuvers in this particular area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I think that main part took out in there [toward Joe Smith's], because it hasn't been after the war and everything went back to normal and people started moving in here, I used to hear of. . . cases where shells were found. They had an artillery they had a rifle range and every kind of a range you could think of down further in the valley, but I don't know what they did up in here, because the buildings are gone, our house was bigger . . . not even a rusty nail left of it, I don't know what they did with it. Probably went over it with tanks and then burned it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Over here on the right again, where Kevin first was looking, there's a. . . it looks like a loading ramp, now that's a side of the Savage Cabin site, right behind you here, due south. Can you see back over in here, you might want to look over this way. See there's a couple dead top trees in there and there's kind of a fence up in there. That looks like they might have loaded logs right in through there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They might have, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think that might be an old logging ramp?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That could be part of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you can't recall anything particular in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the mill, what they were making here is dimension lumber out of second growth fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything about Coote? Maybe we can ask that more when we get towards the house there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What house?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Coote's house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't know much about him. They were. . .they minded their business and everything. They were nice people. In fact, they were. . . I would say under religious diet. But they never bothered anybody and he had financial troubles like any other body did at that time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Depression?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Depression, yes. Sometimes the brokers would change their mind and not. . . see they sold in them days their lumber to brokers. And took the brokers price and then he'd sell it. But they were all right. None of our here in this country here, the way people weren't as closely knitted. If you started pulling crooked deals and things you wouldn't last very long, they'd get you out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One thing to be broke, but another thing to be crooked.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Most of the transportation and markets on the Soap Creek side went into Corvallis, but on this side here where . . . you say your markets were over more towards Salem.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's because Corvallis had no use for pulp wood and that's what we sold. And we sold some . . . we had some contractors would come out and pick up a load of red fir fire wood and take it into town and sell it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Into Corvallis?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Into Corvallis, they didn't haul fire wood as far as Salem, it was too far. We never dealt anything with Monmouth or Independence at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just too far to haul it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Airlie, was there anything in Airlie, any market?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no market in Airlie at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you went to the store where would you go?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We'd go into Corvallis. If we were going to Salem . . . see, we lived out here, we

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: couldn't get out all the time, so we'd go to Salem to get our check at the pulp mill then we'd buy maybe a month's or two's supply there. We didn't have a local Safeway to go to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of vehicle would you take into.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Any kind of a car, we had to wait for the flood waters to die, because you see this creek over here it. . . it practically travels on the top of the ground and you noticed that road that goes in, they put a pan on there. That used to be right on top of the road, it would maybe get that deep and you couldn't get out. I remember the creek that used to be where we lived, it would make such a roar at night you couldn't sleep when the heavy rains. No, that was the way it was, we did go into Salem to get our check and then we'd buy food that would last maybe a month or two.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: D.  The 100 Road

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're here by stop one on the historical tour, let's look off to the east first, do you recall whose barn that is there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say that's Mr. Tandy's barn. That's where the Tandys lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was their house located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The house was just this side of the barn. The house is gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Tandys, did they have any children?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think so. No. He was one of what they called the skinners that worked at the Coote's sawmill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was a Coote's employee?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Coote's employee.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did that house, this was a the Tandy place then, not the Tandy house, would that be correct?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, see I don't know how they got the property or how it was named. But the Tandy's lived there in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any other structure between the Tandy's and the school house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was a family called the Cornutts. They lived between here and that bridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so their. . . between Tandy's and the bridge there was another family. So they lived pretty close together the Tandys and the Cornutts.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the Cornutts have any children?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. I think about three or four or more.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did. . . where did Mr. Cornutts work?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Re also worked with Mr. Coote, he was a brother-in-law.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cornutts and Coote were brother-in-laws?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that lead to any jokes or plays on names or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did the mill workers do for recreation?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Drank beer, go hunting.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So hunting was kind of community, would the people who live here part time socially and associate with the people that lived here year round?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they used to have a community get togethers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The mill workers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, once in awhile somebody would say bring some whiskey or bring some beer and cake and I'll have a fiddler and the house would be big and they'd have a dance and some women would drink coffee and cake and the men would go out in back and sip a keg of whiskey.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had to have something like that or they'd go nuts.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would. . . who's homes would they go to. . . to do that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, any house that was big enough to hold them. Burkes, they had a big house, they were down there just the other side of the bridge. Burkes, they had a farm, he had about a couple hundred acres. And they'd have people coming there and have a good time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Burkes house would be like maybe a major.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Almost like a community place. It was big enough; it had big rooms and everything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would anybody ever go over to Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they never went over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It would just be local get togethers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Everybody kind of stayed in their own area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you say this was more of a milling community while you lived here rather than a farming community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was a mix. See, now Dickeys, they had a farm. And Brinkley that lived over the hill, he had a lot of land down there. I used to drive a tractor for him. And of course, they had their wood lots and things. It was a mixed community, mixed farming and everything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the farmer kind of associate more towards the grange and mill workers associate more towards the mill or did they mix?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were all friendly. They'd all mix together socially.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the farmers would go to the dances too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As well as the sawmill workers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any of the people that played at these.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what kind of music they played?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Either the fiddle or the accordion.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Square dance music?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it's square dance music just like they used to have in Pedee.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they have get togethers out here maybe at the school or was that strictly school and church?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think they had any at the school, I think it was mostly . . . no, because they had hard liquor and I don't think the school board would like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember who made the hard liquor? It's too late for them to get arrested today.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Too late now. Oh, it was mostly only home made beer and stuff like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what. . . would certain families specialize in it or did everybody kind of make their own?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you, not that I'm afraid to, but I couldn't tell you who brought the stuff. It just all at once it was there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: People were kind of were a little bit discreet about it then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they were.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From here can you see where the Polks used to live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lived on the other side of bunch of fir up against that . . . they were up against that hill, the main hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The main hill over there, east most.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The top is shrouded in fog.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was Polk Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's what we called Polk Hill. And that had a lot . . . not this first bunch of trees but way out there it the Joe Smith farm area. There used to be a lake out in there at one time and then he drained it. Where the second row of trees are is where the Joe Smith family lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where we can see buildings now, that was the Joseph Smith place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that was the Joe Smith's place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And there was a lake between here and there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there used to be a lake . . . lot of water drained into it, it was a big marsh and ducks and stuff through there. Now, they've drained that and use it for farm land.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Domestic ducks or wild ducks that stopped there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, wild ducks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was part of the fly way through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there a lot more ducks and geese in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We didn't have many geese out here at all, their main travel route was in the valley and they'd stopped, there wasn't green much here for them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the ducks would come through?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we'd get occasionally what they call a beta wood duck. They'd come up the creek, but now there's no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about through that area then that we just passed, was there a creek or anything that flowed through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I never discovered any creeks of any kind.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You recall. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What I think it was water come out of the ground, big spring.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any Indian sites or any Indian artifacts in the area we just traveled?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I never discovered anything over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is basically a cattle country on this side [north side of 100 road]; over here [south side] this was basically mill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, up in that . . . from this road that way was mostly mill. This was general mixed farming and they had a hard time making a living, I'll tell you that. The soil was poor, now like for instance on the forty acres we lived on, we had a red shot soil around the house and then back away from the house there was about two inches of top soil and shale underneath. The shale was all streaked with black streaks like it one time contained oil. And then down in the creek bottom there was a red hard rock like a red granite that was exposed by the water. It had little tiny crystals in it. It had the feel of rock, of course we had this burned out rock we used to call it, and it looked like iron rock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This road that came through here, was this a rock road at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This road was always like it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And how did. . . what kind of rock, where did the rock come from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know where they got the crushed rock, but it was always rock on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So everything back then looked, except for these building being missing now, everything looked pretty much the same.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The same, in fact they could drive by and I could recognize it right now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's interesting. On Joseph Smith place, those buildings that are out there now, getting fogged in, do you think those are the same buildings, did that look about the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I recall that was approximately the site where the house was but I don't know . . . he had a nice home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the trees that tall at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they were.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the skyline looked about the same. How big was the lake about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it covered about ten acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ten acres.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As I recall it as a natural, kind of like a marsh. And it had a lot of dead trees in it and stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that lake came in after trees did? So maybe the farming had caused the lake?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really don't know, I can remember it was always there though.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Summer time too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would dry up pretty well in the summer but in the winter it would fill up. I think what it was it was a low area and the water couldn't get out. And then it would fill up a great deal in the winter and in the summer it would just gradually fade away.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Did the children play on that if it froze over in the winter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I couldn't tell you, I never went down there when it froze. I don't remember severe freezing up here. The only real . . . we had snow and some cold but it never froze anything solid like it does like in town. Frozen water pipes, we never had that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this creek through here, did you fish it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we used to fish it a lot. Catch nice trout.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what kind?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I used to just call them brook trout fish.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Brook trout.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Them days we didn't worry about technicalities about things. We just . . . it was a fish.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you don't know if it was a cutthroat or a rainbow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It wasn't a rainbow, it might have been possibly a cutthroat. They had a dark spots in their.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big were the fish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, about six to ten inches long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever catch any big ones?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'd catch one that long . . . from .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About a foot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About a foot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They'd go up to about a foot. I asked Glender on the other hill and. . . other side of the hill and he said he caught one once thirteen and a half inches.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, boy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it made an impression. On this creek can you recall salamanders or frogs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. A lot of salamanders, frogs, and snakes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of snakes, garter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Whatever snakes that would swallow a frog.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Large snakes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were about that big.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About an inch and a half diameter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About maybe how long?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About that long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About three foot? Would that be a common garter snake or a different kind of snake?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I recall a common garter snake was black, but these were light colored.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Light brown?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Light brown. In fact, one time I had an experience. I heard something go peak-eap-eap. I was walking along the creek and I wondered what in the sam hill that was. I went down there and there was a frog, he was tugging away and the darn snake had a hold of his leg and was trying to do something to get started to swallowing him, so I just reached down and pinched the side of that snake's jaws and he released the frog. And the old frog jumped into the water and threw the snake in the brush. That was kind of an awful noise the frog made when it was in distress.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, you'd never heard that noise before?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. You said there was a lot of pheasant in those days was that all through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Down in this area here. China. And once in a while they'd come up in here, but they were mostly down here. We used to . . . raise the grain crops like oats, barley, wheat, and it used to be heavy in birds and grass seed and stuff, very heavy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that would be further to our east here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This up in here is pasture because there's more cattle up through here, for cows?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any homes off to the left here, say out where those horses are or anything through this field here that's to our northwest?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I think it was all like it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall who owned it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Recall what?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall who owned this field through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see. In fact they didn't have a gate. I think I do, I think Joe Smith owned a lot of this land up in here. In fact that's where we got a hold of the forty; it was his land. And I think he rented this land out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To other farmers ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now he lived back over in that hill there that we've just been looking at, but he owned a lot of this land.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He owned a lot of this land. Like I say, it's different loggers that lived on houses and I wouldn't be surprised if maybe somebody built the house, they weren't very expensive houses just clapboard built, very flimsy and I wouldn't be surprised if he rented these to loggers around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On these cheap houses that were in here, were they pretty old when you lived here or were they.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ours, when we moved in ours, it was quite old.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they might have been twenty or forty years old?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, according to some of the garbage, you know, stuff we found around the place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But they were kind of. . . weren't main farm houses or anything, they were just more quick built short term houses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. For people to live. . .well, like Tandy's house, they had a house and a barn, maybe he built the house and barn, we never found out whether he bought the property or not. But he had a pretty nice place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He had a pretty nice place, but some of the other places then would be just.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just plain. Nothing to brag about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. Now over here I think you mentioned a Mennonite settlement.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mennonites had a graveyard up on top of that hill there someplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that's what you call Brinkley Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. There was a pioneer graveyard there was about two or three graves. When we left here, they were just about hardly distinguishable. Yeah, the Mennonites at one time lived here once and they moved out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall when they lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I couldn't tell you. Just like I say, see when you move into a neighborhood first thing I started do is ask questions what legends, about old treasure and stuff like that and things gradually keep coming out. Found out about the Mennonites and they moved over to Albany.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you have any feeling for what years they lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. It was a long time ago when they lived here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or how many there were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a colony but I couldn't tell you how many.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was a whole colony. Do you know about where they were located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were in this district here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On both sides of the road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they lived in houses and some farmed and . . . but they moved out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was kind of a wide spread Mennonite colony through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It might have been possibly, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could they have moved out even before the turn of the century or would it have been closer to.

entries.speaker: A
