entries.text: I couldn't tell you anything about that no, see I never took too much interest except what I heard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, on mentioning legends did you ever hear legend of the gold filled boot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any legends of any treasures through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, there was supposed to have been some treasures up on this pass, they used to call it Stage Coach Road or some kind of a road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you call this road when you lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We just called it the county road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The county road, but it used to be called the Stage Coach Road [See Tampico Road], you heard it called that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've heard it called that and there's supposed to be a stage robbed up in that top of that summit someplace. But they don't where . . . there was supposed to be some gold hid somewhere up in the woods, but nobody ever found it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, do you recall any other tales of gold or any gold mines, anybody trying to mine gold

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this is very poor mineral country, all you have here is some jasper and chalsedony and the rest is gravel and quartz, not quartz but. . . no, seriously, I panned up here, I couldn't get any. I used to pan the canyon up where we lived, the timber. Because up there they've got a black rock and it's got white crystals running all through it. But the crystals have no depth, just peel them off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever find any fossils?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, fossils, no fossils except quite a ways north of here in some of these dry washes, I found ancient marine shells and stuff like that. They're quite common through here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In this area, no gold, no fossils, only the one legend of a treasure from the gold stage.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's it and hard work.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're going to be coming back into your old homestead area in the Cootes area there and the Kalapuyan site there a little bit later so I think now we're ready to go on to the.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: E.  Savage Creek Crossing

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, you're talking about the Indians and the creek that ran through here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] He had mentioned that the creek went through here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the creek had diverted and naturally it used to come through those trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Through the trees through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so then it cut out through this field?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Evidently there was a dam or something was put up there, but that's first time I've ever noticed it so deep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We came through here last June.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We're sitting here, we've just crossed the creek and we're looking at the new channel, do you recall when the dam was constructed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, because when we moved here the mill and the dam was there. It was in site.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had this channel worked through the field yet?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it had not. The creek used to come down through those trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this channel has changed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The channel has changed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this meadow off to our left, is the tree line about the same as you can recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, according to the age of trees, them oaks they aren't very young and they've been always there. The firs, they're about fifteen. . . twenty years old. So they could have grown out in the field more.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You talked about walking with your father from your home to the mill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we used to come out of our property, come out of that gate and then cross diagonally across that field. [Meadow on south side of 100 road]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you be up to the timber to our west here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Go right into the mill and then we'd go up in between the mountains to our hundred and sixty acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that trail that you followed in that direction was that a wagon road or a path?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a path, we just established it, see, we just . . . instead of coming down here and going up, we just cut across and established a path and come out by the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was just your family short cut to the mill there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this road we're on right here was this in here at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The road was on the. . . yes, the road was in here at that time, because over there the farmers didn't want to give us any right of way to go out, so we had to use this road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you couldn't get any right of ways through the people on the other side of Berty Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this channel on our left here, that was called the South Fork of Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We used to call that the South Fork of Berry Creek, but some called it Savage. I don't really know what it is now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Only Savage, the only time. . . did you hear that from any source other than me? Did anybody else ever call that Savage? [See Dickey Oral History, Monograph #3]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, you're the only one, but I figured you knew what you were talking about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was using an 1850's map. I was wondered if anybody was still calling it that by 1920. Now this fork here, was this the main Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] This fork of Berry Creek to our right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that was the main fork of Berry Creek, there's no forks on the other side of that. That was the main fork and then there's another one up in the hills that comes down

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and runs into it, but it's a much smaller creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Do you know anything about these timbers, those timbers that are sitting in that field right there, was there a structure here? Or are those just old logs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think those are just old logs, no, there was no structure there. All the Dickey property was on the other side of that creek, and this was the after land. And along through here and close to the creek is where they used to find the Indian bowls and arrowheads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that on this side of the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On both sides of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On both sides of the creek, about where we are right now, is the site.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, because I think it was . . . for summer camps.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think that this area to our right and on both sides of the creek was the summer camp site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you describe some of the materials that were found in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was like pieces of bowls, like that out of stone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ten or twelve inches in diameter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About like that, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the pestles next to the stones?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were scattered about and then the burred arrowheads I have are about that long and that wide, I found those in. . . in fact used to take a shovel and dig all day where you'd find the darn things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this area out here would you find them all the way up to the road here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not that far back, oh, maybe thirty or forty feet from the creek bank.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On both sides?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you 'dfind mortars and pestles and arrowheads about an inch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, would you find obsidian arrowheads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were all obsidian.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All of them obsidian.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I gave. . . I found four of them and I gave them to my nephew in Kiamath Falls. Burred points.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you find any mortar and pestles yourself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, but we never bother just with . . . they were something common, put by a doorstop or something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were just used for doorstops?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you see any nice mortars and pestles that maybe some of the neighbors had collected?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, they. . . everybody had something. Set on the porch and put flowers in them or something . . . grow some flowers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were kind of used for flower pots and doorstops and.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you're talking about Indian burial practices, did you ever find any burial sites through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Sometimes I'd find high mounds but digging in to them, I found out it was just an old stump, tree had fallen over and the stump had rotted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you could find mounds around here, but it would be wind throw?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wind throw.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any signs of structures or anything of that nature from the Indians?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you talked about a path that crossed and we visited that site where the water coming on Berry Creek goes from a shallow and then forms a deep canyon and you said that was the old bridge site or crossing site there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now was that the western most boundary of the Indian signs. . . what. . . where was the western .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Most of the Indian signs started right down in this area here

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right about where we are?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And then that meadow. Out in our land, we dug and had the fields plowed and everything for garden and we never encountered a thing. Mostly down below here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would you clear these fields here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you'd. . .we used to take and dig them out and take a horse and pull out the wild roses and put a chain around them and drag them out. And then this area just burn some of the stumps.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there many stumps through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, this . . Dickeys had cleaned off a lot of land, this was mostly oak trees through here and we had our creek just like a park, cleaned off all the brush and stuff and we could walk along there and see the water.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How do you think this looked, say, around 1900, was it. . . was this forested through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: 1900, that was before I was born.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, that's why I'm asking for a guess here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I think this was pretty well all open and the trees seeded themselves and advanced.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the stumps you were clearing out were from younger trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Younger trees. Mostly oaks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so it was oak seeding in from larger oak back on the hills here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so, I think they . . . the wind blew and storms.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did any of these hills or ridges have names back in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. No nicknames.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nothing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No nicknames.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just the hills.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just the hills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Until we got over to Forest Peak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Polk Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Polk Hill and then Brinkley Hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Brinkley Hill, that was the three main ones.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you talked about a horse camp coming down this little valley, western valley to the main road here, a horse trail. The last time we talked. That they had signs of a horse camp

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: over in here, where people camped out and rode horses.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'm trying to think just exactly what that group was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did people ride horses around here in the 1930's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, some people had saddle horses, they'd ride them around and go one place to another.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any of the routes they might have taken through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they just went across any place, there wasn't a lot of fences in here at that time. This was all open. And this was . . . there was no fence here except over towards the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the. . . this area up through here was just pretty much open pasture land?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Except for this road here? Was this road rock?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, this road was always . . . well, at one time it wasn't . . . in fact, we had have a horse, a team to get us in our car to the house. We'd get stuck in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the road have a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it did not. No name to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this Kalapuyan site over to the right here, did that have a name? Would you call.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it wasn't called like "scenic meadows" or anything, it was just a place where the Indian one time camped.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I marked the Hanish, I marked the Hanish Site, would it be more appropriate to name it after the land owners that were in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you could probably call it the Dickey Site.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dickey Site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: D-i-c-k-e-y.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's how you kind of think of it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, because that was on their property.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And this road here, would it have any particular name, do you recall at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was just a connecting road to get back to the people that lived back there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you. . . the Dickey's lived here on the right and then your family was here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Dickey's lived over in there and we lived well, in fact. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the map, flip the page over. [Refers to map]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We'll take it this way. Here's the Coote's house. Starting in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We'll be going back over there probably right towards the end.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And on the road that goes back up in here and it just keeps going, back in here and to the right, the Dickey's lived in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had a big house and a big barn. And then you . . . several hundred yards, the road stopped and then it went this way, but this was our fence and our house was in here and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the Hanish house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the Hanish house. And this road here it disappears . . . it turns and goes right at this fence and somewhere along here, I noticed there is an old road, I think that's what happened. This road bypasses it, but I rode from our house across the creek and the bridge and we came out here about the same distance the Dickey's is and then it turned and come down into this road here. But the other time we was here, I noticed there is an old road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up in here and that's the original road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you think of anything else in this area. . . how about these trees up through here, did they. . . we're looking west, do they look about the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About the same, the timber's about the same height and everything, maybe a little bit taller, but it was always there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The main changes might be the fences, and the creek channel?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of anything on this site, anything else?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Did you find any material out on this side, on the left, in tenns of the Indians?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. In fact, I never really looked for anything except what we found over here. I used to go along like for instance a bank of a creek, not that one, but our creeks and I'd look along in the soil strata to see if there was anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] In the winter did this get pretty swampy out in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it didn't get too swampy but the creek itself would just about ready to go over the bank. It was quite high.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] So if the Indians happened to be through here late spring or fall and if there was good rains, would you think they would be over here on this rise at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's very possible they could be over there, plan a test dig, but they mostly came up here in the heat of the summer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's what you heard that they migrated in here when it was hot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And then in the fall too, they'd stay in the summer and the fall to get their deer, their meat. I don't know where they lived in the valley, I guess they lived along the main river down there someplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Don't you think more up around where those storage pits are?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: These areas where there was deer and that, that you can recall at that time, were there a lot of deer in this country?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they weren't too thick, but there were deer. I could see one at least every other day if I was out running around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ever recall any eagles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Never saw an eagle? How about owls, were there a lot of owls?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very few. Very few owls, once in awhile you'd hear one hoot at night and that would be about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about hawks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we had what they call the Super hawk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Super hawk?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he'd be flying around. And red tail hawk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you see those fairly often?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not too often.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why do you think that was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was . . . to me it was just a hawk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would the farmers like them, or. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they liked them because they would go over and they'd get the ground squirrels. And the ground squirrels of course would make a lot of holes in the ground and imperil the livestock and everything else. In fact, it used to be the Sunday sport to go out and shoot them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ground squirrels?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Take your .22 out and shoot them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about coyotes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At that time there were no coyotes in here. People had sheep and there were no deaths caused by coyotes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any talk of bear or cougar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I've hunted through all these hills and I've never seen a sign of a bear. . . one old man said he did once but . . . they probably wandered in from the coast range across Kings Valley and come into here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cougars have a long travelling range too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you've never heard of any or saw any sign?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you were telling me before about brush bunnies, could you describe those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they were small, about eight inches long, four or five inches wide and they have coarse black hair or fur on them. We found them in brush piles and they'd live off of trees and things . . . make wood or something. We'd pile the brush in a pile for burning. Well, we'd go to burn, I hit the pile with a stick to scare them out of there and there'd be three or four of them, but you only found them up on the top of the. where our timber was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Only the high elevations.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: High elevations.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they real common up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Didn't see them, only except for they'd hide in the brush and we'd scoot them off. They might have been a nocturnal thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you shoot them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no. I didn't shoot them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they afraid of people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I meant shoo them out. No, they were not very timid, you could pick them up, they

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You could go along and pick them up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they didn't bother to scratch you or anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about jack rabbit, were there any jack rabbits?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there were a few jack in through here. And jack and ground squirrels, hawks, occasional pheasants, and up in the timber is what they call flying squirrels.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you see very many flying squirrels?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't see them, but I seen the remnants of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were pretty common?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I don't know how many there was, but they were up there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: F.  130 Road

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we're on the 130 Road, come up a new stretch where the old road used to cut over to your house, and we've come up above the meadow where you used to hike over to the mill. And we're going to start angling towards Forest Peak on a road that none of us have ever been on before, so we're going to be lost here but we should be up somewhere around your one-sixty [160 acres], I'm thinking, because we've come about a mile and a half or two miles up the creek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So are you oriented enough to say anything about this or are you lost enough to just. . . that we should drive on a little bit further?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know anything at all about this country here.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: G.  South Fork Bridge

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we're on the South Fork of Berry Creek, right here. Now the old road as you came up from Coote's mill into this country here. You say it followed on the right hand side of the creek which would be right in front of us here. Being on the south side of the creek. Is this the old. . . do you think this is the old road bed going right in front of us here, or was the bridge somewhere below us or can you tell for sure?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that's . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would we be about back on your family's one-sixty in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, you're not far enough up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think it's still further up to the west here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was practically straight, the family place was practically straight south from the Coote's sawmill up that canyon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Through that draw that you showed me where the trees came together?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Okay, that would put that in that track over there, because this is the bridge over here to my left, at this angle and I would think that we're pretty much on that break.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're in that canyon that you were pointing to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Let me get up here a little bit and see if this is the road right here. [Couldn't locate old road bed.]

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part II.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: April 10, 1990: Forest Peak Tour

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: H.  Forest Peak

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm going to put this recorder on here. These are the ones you described?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. These are the ones.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well I'm going to have to take yours and Kevin's picture, I know that. All right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] They're about two feet deep?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they were about three feet deep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Were there any kind of cultural materials laying around?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just those. I even dug a little bit in the bottom to see if anything. . . couldn't find anything but rock. And nothing around them at all. Not any kind of implements were down here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But this is it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The wrong . . .. that was ten or fifteen years before the war, I was up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who was the old man that told you about these?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Old man Brinkley, he passed away.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Brinkley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had the Brinkley . . . you know on your map the Brinkley Hill?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes. We put that on your word.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the Brinkley farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK We'll be going through that today, too. See where the huckleberries encroaching here and we've got fawn lilies here. This must have been more prairie even when you saw it before?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did it look like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Another fellow and I, we used to hunt graydiggers, we used to come up here, we used to sit on the side of the hill, eat our lunch, shoot graydiggers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is Forest Peak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, this is Forest Peak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] So this forest area over here was open, in the south east direction this was open

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: out in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Prairie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was all prairie down below there and on the side of the peak it was prairie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Do you know the names of any of the creeks that come off of here?)

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there wasn't . . . I didn't know of any creeks. Let's see the creek that. . .. get my damned directions here, that's south, isn't it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Yes, sir.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, our timber holdings were over there because Forest Peak was. . . we'd go up to our timber holdings on our left, there was a creek come down through a canyon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right down through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think we called it Savage Creek. We used to call the left fork of Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. That's right down below us here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's source was up on . . . see, there's a steep canyon between our timber holdings and this range through here, but that creek ran through the canyon and it come out at the base of the hill where our road went up over and we built a bridge in there so the water could go down . . . the last time [February hike with Kevin] we walked up through there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The creek would be to our left . . . to our right, way over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Correct.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We didn't get up to where we had built the bridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But since we've talked to you last, we've got some 1936 aerial photos so we should be able to trace them right out on that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] That last route that you and I attempted to take to get up here, right down over here through these trees is the upper end of that, and it's a well used game trail from here and I walked down there and we were pretty close to it that day.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But this is it, here's the [Indian] pits. There's one of those firs you see from the highway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK, now these fir here that are cut down, these you used to see these from Highway 99?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that's how you could tell this was Forest Peak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And the top of the peak is kind of all broken up. You can see tree tops and naked tops and.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, it's kind of scraggly old oak and old fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. There's one old timer up here wasn't very high, but it was really storm worn. The limbs were way down low like you find on the coast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Like that one down right over there? [Indicates downed Douglas-fir tree.]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Find on the coast, that probably was one of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Down in this direction here is Berry Creek, now from here where did you find that obsidian bi-face?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I found that . . . let's see, come up the road, follow that creek up, there was a road that went back up through there, come to this bridge, start up a steep hill, very steep, in fact the logging trucks had a hell of a time getting up there with their trailers and just about half way down is where I found that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let me take a few pictures of you next to the pits, there too. Can you think of anything else you want to ask on the recorder right now?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Not right at this moment.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok. When was the last time you were up at this site here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was about 1935. Of course we lived down on the forty acres for a number of years and I didn't get up here right away. And it was around 1935 I was on top of the peak and found the pits.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Put this on again. Did you ever come up here deer hunting?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I never hunted deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the route we're looking at on the south face, did you ever use that route?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever come up just straight up the ridge line from Writsmans Hill down there or. Smith Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up to this peak?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes. Did you ever just by taking the ridge. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never approached it from that angle, always approached it from the road that went up to our timber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that just because that's your property or was that the main trail up here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that alley. Well, that was the original road that was built up here by. . . long time ago for to cut lumber and stuff. I mean wood for the mills. That's

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] The old logging roads do come all the way up on the back side, the north side here. Now, they're reduced pretty much to just a game trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. Which reminds me on the picture there you can see they've logged through it, but it looks like that could have been part of a forest fire. Was that. . . did they have any forest fires through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they had fire one year we was out here, they had to bring out fire fighters from Oregon State to fight it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that right over down below us here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was down below.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was before 1936?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I couldn't tell you the exact year, but in that period when we lived here, it probably could be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any other forest fires in the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we had one that came down into our forty from the west. But they called from the Kings Valley side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall the year?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could have been around 1930 or 1932?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I thought it was around 1928, 1929. Because see I . . . that was about the time I was getting ready to go down to California to go to work. And I left then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was right before 1930 a Kings Valley fire came from the west.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How much ground did that cover over there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I really don't know, they had the 3-C boys out fighting it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, that would have had to been after 1932, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. It probably would have been.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] After 1933.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Roosevelt started the CCC, NRA, Social Security and the whole works.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There used to be a big rock someplace in here, used to sit on, but I don't see it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] I remember you saying that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Large rock, it's probably got covered up with soil.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they ever had a trail down this ridge line here, did they run game, sheep, or anything up in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never noticed. See, we used to live down on the other side and this friend of mine, he lived in our neighborhood and we used to come from that side and we'd sit up here and shoot greydiggers on those slopes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Well, there's some big rocks over here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably . . . I used to bring people up here . . . when they'd come out there. Well, like the Stevens family, they had two daughters that were . . . come out every summer and see them and I used to bring them up here. In fact, I brought a whole party of six one time that wanted to see the top. And of course at that time, the pits were open and no brush or nothing in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you used to kind of show them off to people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Kind of like. . .. kind of a guide in this district.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got this thing going again. This has got one hundred and twenty-one rings at about five years of age. So it's about 125 years old. That would put it. . . and it's been logged about five years ago. So it's about 130 years old. That would put it at 1860, which would be the 1850, 1860 right after settlement pattern. These trees came in from maybe some of those old growth right up on the knob there and Jim, you're saying these size of trees here, this hundred year old size class is what you used to call old growth?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So trees this big you'd say were an old growth tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We called those old growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It has limbs in there, the smaller ones we'd call them second growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. So an old growth tree might have only been. . . Kevin and I saw some that were seventy that were this big or larger and this had most of its growth by the time it was seventy-five or eighty, so you could have had hundred year old trees that you were calling

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: old growth back in the 1930's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. Like I told Kevin here, we had some that took us two and a half hours to fall, they were that big of tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would be the same age class as this group here in a better site.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] He was telling us they used to cut shakes out of them for barns and what not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Out of this size here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Made the best shakes there is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would this be what you call red fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Red fir. Red or Douglas, I'm not sure, but it's not a hemlock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We just called it red fir, old growth, second growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I have one more question here for you, I keep forgetting, you said when you were talking with Jan [Meranda] and I, that there was sheep with curly-q horns that you found back up in the drainages, can you kind of point where that was and describe them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they used to have . . . you know where we were on the forty acres that we thought was the forty acres above Dickeys and up through there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pretty closely, yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I used to go right straight up west through the woods and head for that, what we called the Kings Valley Ridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] That's it right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be the Kings Valley Ridge in front of us?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There used to be an old gentleman that had a cattle ranch back up in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be the Kings Valley Ridge that one going right up the middle right down to Beriy Creek there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. That's good. Do you know what that big high ridge behind is named?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We used to call that Coast, that's the other side of Kings Valley, that's the coast ridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] The high ridge back there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, wouldn't that be on this side of Airlie wouldn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see now, this ridge here . . . that's not Kings Valley ridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, Kings Valley would be over this way.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Kings Valley is the other side of that big ridge over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. I was thinking Kings Valley would be this way here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: These goats or whatever you want to call them, they were found all through that. a rancher had them, used to just let them run wild. He harvested the wool.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But then they went wild?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were domestic sheep that went wild. They had a curled horn. The horn came out and curled . . . no they weren't, they were wild if they'd see you, but they weren't wild game.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He took care of them then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he had a ranch and took care of them. And lot of times it happened, people had homesteads, they'd leave and leave the stock to forage for themselves. Then they did go into a wild stage.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] That's due west over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok. So that would be Kings Valley Ridge over there. And then this ridge in between.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This ridge. . . that ridge over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the Coast Ridge, and this is the Kings Valley Ridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: I.  The Dickey Farm

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They'd be to our left.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] So, this hill then through. . . just through this gate probably would have been the site where the original house was for the Dickeys and this

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had a house and barn and . . . it was just like our places, there wasn't a thing left, not even a board.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] And you feel pretty comfortable that this is the probably the route you would have taken?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. One of the ways until we were shut off. Then we walked around and went down near the side of the creek up there on that other road. And the road getting into there was on the left hand. . . going up on the left hand side of Berry Creek and then we'd cross.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Jim feels that this rise right here might have been where the old Dickey house and barn and stuff sat out in there. This is probably the lane that they'd use to walk up until Dickeys made them go around the other way, when they'd go to get their mail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK, did you record that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] It's all on tape and it's going now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I used to walk down through here to

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm recording you right now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] I'm going to go down here and take a look at this.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You want to go down there too Jim?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got this tape recorder. We're standing on the Dickey site here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is about where the Dickey house was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. We're standing next to a flowering quince. That little draw have a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's just a little valley that runs on down . . . there used to be a family live down there below, the Stevens family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Stevens lived down there, maybe about where that field was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Then we was at the Hodgson place once before, we went off over in there someplace and the Hodgsons was up on the hill where all those oak trees were cut. And all that poison oak was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. We should be driving by there. We've got the Stevens down below us and then. Hanishes were right up here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, Hanishes were up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. Then down here was the Cootes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dickeys and then Cootes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is Dickeys here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is the Dickey site here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And where we came up in the car there, we were following pretty much what used to be a foot path.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, foot path or a road. There used to be a road through there but. . . like I was telling Kevin, the Dickeys didn't want us coming down through there to get our mail,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: so we went out across the bridge and down the other side and back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To the Coote's mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, to pick up our mail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, you walked all the way around to get your mail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEViN] Their mail was down by the Cornutts house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Dickeys told them not to come through here, so they had to go out and around.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We're about like the Hatfields and McCoys. Only we didn't shoot each other.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just didn't cooperate much.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know they had any outhouses, they had a great big house . . . probably didn't they had a barn, a good size barn, that's probably what's down in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've got a couple depressions here, do you have any ideas if this was a root cellar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, like I say, we weren't friendly with them, we weren't too much around the place. But they did have a big barn, they had a team, farmed the all this land. They used to farm right up to our fence.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That archeological site, that's. . . right over there, just from that meadow on over.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably from anywhere, we could

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All along the creek there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Take test holes. Sift it out and might find an arrowhead.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEViN] I'd like to drive out there towards Jim's old place, maybe look at the creek out around there and then. . . go back over here where ever we need to go.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Right up through there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Somewhere in those trees on that slope, when we were here they were all overgrown. They're probably gone now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was a pioneer cemetery?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Children's graves.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you have any idea who was buried there, would it have been the Berry family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, any was there was settled before any the Mennonites of the Bookinites or something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you don't know their names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had little tiny things come up like that and their names were ......

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that would be back on the road there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, back just up in that grove of fir and oak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] North by Northeast from the Dickey homestead.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: J.  Hanish Homestead

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jim, we're on the site of your old home right now and we're looking at bricks and mound, blackberries but this is the location of your old farmhouse.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: in the painting you've got of the barn, it's directly behind you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it was up by the creek there, on the creek. Should be maple trees in behind it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You say these maple trees in front, in those days they were just.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just saplings.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: in those days they planted these maple trees so they'd have living fence posts, so they wouldn't have to keep putting in fence posts?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember who planted those maples?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were in. . . probably Joe Smith planted them, they were in here. I know we used to have an unbroken view of the valley from the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said, at night you could see the trains there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What trains would those be?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Southern Pacific.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On a clear day you could see mountains, there's a snow capped peak in the Cascades? I don't know if it's Mount Baker. . . not Mount Baker, but Mount Washington, just the mountain that's south of Mount Hood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But right in the center, as you look at down the valley, see those trees along the creek, they've grown up a lot but we could see Suver and Wren and you could hear the trains, the lights of the trains.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Suver and where else?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wren, remember Wren.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I thought Wren was over on the Kings Valley side.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not Wren, another little town.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You're thinking of. . . Wells.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There used to be a town called something like that. It was just east of Mountain View. And it was this way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it Wells, Wells Station?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Might have been, but it . . . Wren sounds familiar . . . but anyway, that's . . . you can't see the mountain.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's April 10th, is this smokier than you remember when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we had a dust storm one time come from Eastern Oregon over here, it was yellow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, you could see it coming and instead of brown like dust it was kind of yellow, funny color. And when it came over here, it deposited a lot of white . . . it looked like sulphur dust.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Out here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All over. We used to . . . it was up in the mountains, we'd fall a tree and we'd have to get away from it, because there just be a cloud of that crap come down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they write about it in the newspapers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They didn't write about it. We . . . now, it would cause panic activity. I would say it might have been from a volcano.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would be 1930's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, way back there. But it was . . . the neighbors thought it was just a dust storm, but the funniest damned dust I ever seen. It just, it had to have come over the Cascades.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's lots of it left there, you could have seen the Dickey family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dickey family, now there's the hill . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Over here, you can see the flowering quince is over there on the ground behind the house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right over there. And beyond that up on that knoll where that oak and stuff was, above the barns, would be the cemetery.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So right on that knoll up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The highest point?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: North toward the highway but it's in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. Now where the barn is, was that barn there in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Which barn?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Down there now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's Oregon State's Barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, so that's a new one.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's new.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then the house that's there

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Coote's house was originally, always there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it always called the Coote's house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, not called the Coote's house, but that's where the owner of the sawmill lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK. And then between him and Dickeys.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dickey's lived right over there, the house and barn and everything, and they tilled this land.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right in front of us.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right in front of us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What were the crops they raised?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it was mostly oats.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oats.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They raised a lot of oats in here at that time. Oats, and then on the other side they raised wheat. In the other valley other there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have an orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had a small orchard around the house, but I see it's all gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, did you have an orchard here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we had an orchard, we had prunes, plums and pears, and our barn was about over in there. Just about. Not quite that far, but the whole thing's gone, they even took out the fir trees that were here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's what we were looking for last time; for the fir trees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The times before when I come out here with my mother, the fir trees were still there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Did you have a crossing, a foot bridge on the creek here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had a regular bridge that we could drive over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Where was that in relation to us?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Over here maybe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If I can find the. . . it was over in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We walked that out before, I think we did. We can probably find it pretty easy. It connects into an old road system, connects into the 100 Road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had this looking like a park, there wasn't any brush in there at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So all these blackberries, there wasn't any of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] This looks like this might have been where the crossing came up here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. This is the crossing where we built a bridge, bring the logs down, put a team of horses and drag them across to the bank.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Last time you were out here, were there any indications of anything left or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] All gone.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No bridge was left, the [U.S. Army] service took everything out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From the bridge down is where they. . . actually from this a little ways down there on down, is where old the Dickey artifacts were found.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I never looked in here, I never thought much of Indian stuff then, because we were trying to make a living with timber and stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you raise in these fields out here? We're looking southwest.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We didn't raise anything, we had stock, we had some cattle, cows, we took sheep on shares, . . . there's a coyote. [Listens to howling]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, how did you keep all the blackberries cleaned off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we just grubbed them out, we didn't let them get a start. And our biggest curse here is what they call a wild rose.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We'd try to dig them out and a long chain on a horse and pull them out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wild rose or any other name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wild roses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sweet briar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sweet briar, they'd blow a hole in the. . . there was always a yellow jacket nest in the woods.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you looked out when you lived here before were those old oak trees, those firs that are on top of the oak now, were they that tall or could you see mostly oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was mostly. . . they were about that tall, they haven't grown much. The barn was right up in there, it wasn't too far from the house. The house was real pretty, it was a short distance.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were also talking about the pond up on the mill, you said they had that funneled and you say you also had a dam in here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we had a. . . it was only about that high,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About two feet.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Backed up the creek. The last time I came out it was gone. I think what happened, it was either this creek here in the winter time is a raging torrent, in fact we couldn't sleep at night on account of the noise it made when we lived here. So it probably since nobody used it, they just took it out or filled it up with debris and that was it. We used to have a . . . gravity. See those coppice trees up in there, that's just about where the dam was. We had this ditch running down . . . this was all garden. We had cherries, prunes, apples, pears.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But none of those trees are left now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you were going through the Depression.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we went through the Depression.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it feel like a Depression to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, for the prices that we got out of things, yes. But we did, we survived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We walking through a bunch of wild strawberries here, did you ever pick those or use any of the native berries around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we had our own. We had a nice big bed of them, we raised our own berries.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you never used any wild strawberries or blackberries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never shot a deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How come you didn't shoot deer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had all the meat we wanted. We used to like to watch them. They used to feed with the cattle out in this . . . this is where the bridge was. I don't know why they took it out. I used to catch trout in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You could catch trout up this high?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of trout were they, do you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember if. . . it was just trout to us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think we've had this conversation before, I was trying.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were about that long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nine, ten, eleven inches.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How far up the valley could you catch them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I used to go up as far as our fence and then it got too ripply, nothing but ripples. They all like the holes farther down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Jim, you're familiar with chert? You know what chert looks like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Well, they'd, some people call it jasper.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, like. . . lot of that in here like jasper and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Yeah. Do you know where the source of this material is in this area, have you ever come across an outcrop of this kind of stuff around here? See the Indians would use a lot of that material, they call it Cryptociystalline silicas, the kind of quartz like the chalsedony is, but I'd be interested if you knew where a source of this stuff might be, it had to get here in the creek somehow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: How does this run -- in strata or is it just loose like gravel?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Well, in this case, like you find in here, you 'dfind it as cobbles and pebbles and. what not, but usually you find it as thick veins and black sedimentary deposits.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now if this was the ridge there used to be a vein of red rock that come out from one of those trees and went out in the water there and had crystals in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Right over by these trees here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, right in there, it might be up in gravel, but that's where it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that might be a source of lithic material here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Correct.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, up in the hills, way away from here I found a rock about that big . . . full of white crystals and that thing would just cut glass like beeswax.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Only one I found.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that's back here in these hills?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was to the left of the going down to the valley that you're talking about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Stevens?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Stevens, it was up on the hill over by Stevens.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's evidence of an old fire through here in that maple. Do you recall any fires or does anybody burn the fields through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No we didn't have any fires at all, evidently it happened when we were gone. Because we had this all cleaned off, you could walk all along this creek we used to keep a crock jar down in there and keep our butter and milk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was kind of like your refrigerator here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you called this left hand of Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We used to call this the right hand, because up there the road crossed the meadow and went out and another creek would come down and we called that the other fork of Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You called that the left hand?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it came out of a swamp up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you fished with worms underneath these little cut banks like this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they're what they call . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you fished with flies sometimes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. Yes, this thing makes so much noise in winter you couldn't sleep sometimes at night, it would be way up . . . up to the top of that bank, just a raging torrent because there were so many curves that the thing would. . . had too much

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: resistances to it would just power over the whole works.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would salmon ever run up this fork?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we didn't. . . no. Yes, that's a nice hole. [Looking down into creek]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're on what you called the south meadow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, the south meadow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: OK, there's a flowering cherry tree there, that be a wild cherry wouldn't it, would that have been anything to do with the family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that was there when we were here, that's right. Like I said, in that country there, there were orchards all through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Up through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Through that wilderness.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what were those orchard from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Homesteaders.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Before your time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, oh, yes, because I used to go up in there, I'd find remnants of an old shack and two or three trees around, evidence of where deer were eating on the fruit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, and that's just straight back from us right up here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, back anywhere in the . . . two, three, four, five miles. I used to walk all through here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall about how many orchards might have been in that country?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I must have found at least three of four.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Three or four? Those wouldn't be the Mennonite orchards though would they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what race they were, just people who came out and settled and they couldn't make it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All gone. Go out through there and around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this would be the road that went back to the old homesteads, that would be to our south. And then the old road used to come across the field here to your.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Our road used to come down from the house, across the bridge, go right through here, following and make a left turn and head to have bunch of trees across the creek, come through the meadows and come to Berry Creek then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, then this creek that came through here, when we went through last time it was dry.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But did it ever dry up when you were a.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Is there an old road that went off? Out that way, did your road come around like this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Our road crossed the . . . crossed the creek, went through here, around the trees and into . . . went through there and across the trees and out . . . out to the highway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Ok, from what I saw, there was possibly your old road, do you know why this is all broken in here where this first trees are in the brush and then there's another clearing and then a bunch of dirt.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there a creek used to . . . in the wintertime there was a. . . see that row of. clump of stuff way over there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was a creek that only run in winter, it come down through there, and then it would run out over into the other creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Did it have. . . big mound of dirt and stuff?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, eroding.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On that creek there, we didn't get that on the end of the tape, but you said it would dry up part of the year and start.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Get dry in the summer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where the head waters of it at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it just came out of the hill up there, probably a spring.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A marsh, was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The marsh was down lower.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Isee.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] You can kind of see where it heads back up over in that there, so it's low and then down over here, you can see where the cattle walked through it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is it running now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think was just a drain, because it would dry up in summer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jim was saying back this way for four and five miles is a bunch of old homesteads with old apple orchards, right off in this direction, and this old road use to go right through there. [KEVIN] Isn't that the 100 road right off over there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, that's where we're going, right?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: IKE VINJ Well, we'd have to go back out and hit the 100 road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There isn't . . . road right up that God forsaken country up in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, that's

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That old maple?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was big when you were a kid, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was big when we were out here. The bank was steep there. And this is where the barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is the. . . the barn was right on this flat here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Next to the maple. Do you know who built the barn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the barn was here when we bought the place. I don't know whether Joe Smith built it or whether . . . who had the property he bought off, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year did you paint it about? [Painting donated to OSU Research Forests]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I painted it. . . let me see, I didn't paint here, I didn't take up oil painting until I got married. Then I went up to the high school and took an art class up there. And then I draw them from my mother's album, she has some old pictures of this place, she's got a picture of the barn and a picture of that field over there. And so I took the picture and painted it. The barn's about that big according to the picture. You can have the whole thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would be great.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had it a long time and wife says give to him, you know, also give him the book about the Applegate Trail because it don't deal with this country at all, it's all California and north. I used to oil paint quite a bit. Now, I kind of concentrates too much on what's .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Your mom's photo album, does she still have those photos?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think she still has them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, would it be possible maybe to make duplicates of those photos too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know if she's still got the prints or not. You can have the photos if you want them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think the archives would be interested.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, we're right next to the Dickey homestead here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're looking south.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we're looking north east.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: North east.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Actually, it's a little bit north west.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then those hills back there, you said they always looked about the same amount of timber?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About the same, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about those fields in the foreground?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was always just pasture, they never raised anything in here that

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about that green field back there up against the firs, was there a field back in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just pasture. Raising livestock.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's a man you may want to call that's down in the [Willamette] Valley. He's a [Berry Creek] boy . . . school, sawmill up there at one time.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: K.  Pioneer Cemetary

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that always a jungle down there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I think that's part of the. . . down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that cemetery is up on this knoll here somewhere?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you describe again how they marked the different markers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, as I can remember, I. . . is that they weren't stone, they had an old picket fence around and it was pretty well shot then. And there were only about two or three graves and they were children. They probably was recorded at the county courthouse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said they burned the names and stuff into the wood markers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. They probably might have used a hot iron, they didn't have any stone that they could use.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Somewhere around the top on the. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Till you get an archeologist digging around for them.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: L.  Coote's House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jim, this is the place you call you the Coote's place here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We used to call it the Coote's house, that's where they lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And was this. . . this driveway here, was this the road that came out here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This road was here and that road was always there, it's a county road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, how about that fruit tree over there, is that part of an orchard or do you remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was always there as far as I remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember an orchard through this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Most every house. . . home had an orchard of some sort. Either apple or pear or. every . . . the first thing they did was plant some trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, how about across the road, was anybody living there at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there was a family, there was two families, there was the Byrd family, they lived down further and then there was the Tandys, he lived over in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where that house is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where the trees are and stuff. There underneath the trees. That's where the Tandys lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He used to work for Coote and he also. . . the school teacher used to teach here at the school house, she used to board with the Tandys and of course the young men would go down there at night and try to visit with her so that Mr. Tandy had to put up examinations so they wouldn't all start courting the school teacher.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember her name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, Lord, no. I was interested too, but hell, I didn't have any chance at all. She was always pretty, always had a pretty school teacher.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Byrd ranch were down there ahead and we just passed. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They tore out that all out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, the Tandys is just that little tiny place in here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a little homesite?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a little homesite.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We just passed an orchard back there on the right would that have been the Tandy's orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I couldn't tell you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok. Then the Tandys would they have been right in. . . to our right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, this is where the Byrd house is right in here, that big oak base, that's where the Byrd homestead was, and the Tandys was over the other way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Between Byrd and the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, and then the Byrd ranch went out this way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it extended all the land from there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, what was the next place here on the left, who was the next person up on the left here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Raintree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the right who was the next person?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't any on the right. There's no houses on the right until you get to the road that goes out to the highway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: M.  Brinkley's House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We just went by the orchard, the Brinkley's orchard there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, Brinkley's orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the gate that says no hunting, that was the entrance to their.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And where was their home located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was right in between those bushes there you see. It wasn't very far off the road. Right in all the brambles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Where the orchard is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's where it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the Brinkleys owned on the left hand side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They owned that and they owned all this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, on the front here too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know how many acres but he had a large mountain of land. Because there used to be a. . . old man Brinkley, he leased it out to a fellow that used to run sheep on shares here in the valley, I can't remember his name now. I used to go down and visit an old codger who lived in there. We used to take our horses and go out and round up the sheep, they'd be all over that country.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All this country through here have trees on it then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no. This was all pastureland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All that oak hill up through there on.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The whole schbang. There wasn't any of those trees then at all. This is all new.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was all sheep grazing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All grazing around here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sheep, cattle, whatever.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: N.  Gross' House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This house here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Was the old Gross family,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And it was the last family between Brinkley and their road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not the last family, but they're the last family between the road that goes down to the valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Last family between Brinkleys and.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, when you cross over the hill, then you start running into one family right after the other.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this in the right was still Brinkley's land though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this belonged to the Gross family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Gross.

entries.speaker: A
