entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: O.  Airlie

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see we're by the. . . flag post in downtown Airlie.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: John [Wienert] . . . store.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the store was here on this flat in front of the grey house on our. . east here? How about that brick building, do you recall that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it's been there a long time, but I don't know what it was used for. It's got a sign on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] It's an old gas station. There's a shell sign and zero.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right, he did have a gas station by gosh. He did start that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was his name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wienert, John Wienert.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've passed McKibbons place, and we couldn't see the house there, do you recall the names of any other families living in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not one. There used to be an old church, community church here but I see that's gone. Probably not enough people went to it so they destroyed it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Now, that looks like a refurbished old building there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the red barn there, is that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It don't ring a bell. That might have been there, and I never paid any attention to it. They've reroofed it, I can see that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So most of your travel went towards Salem, it didn't come up Airlie area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Salem and towards Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are you familiar with this road in front of us here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Maxfield Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: P.  Staats Creek

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see we're in an orchard at the end of Paul Dunn Forest Road at a marshy turn around, right?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] You can't hardly see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jim, did this valley here have any name to it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it didn't, as far as I know, it didn't have any name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have a road through it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, trying to think where in the hell we're at now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Well, Stevens would have been right down there to your right, back up in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was no road through this valley. There was just as it is. The only road was accessed off the main gravel road to the homes that lived along back on the edge of this valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: County road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: County road and then down in there, the road that came in that was facing down there, the Hoovers and the Cox place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Hoovers and Cox, but they had a road coming in off the county road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Their road came into the road that we had come in to begin with that said dead end. That was the original road that went in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To the Hoovers and the Coxes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, that's the one marked Paul Dunn Forest.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] The one that's got the orchard by it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and then down the county road there was the Brinkleys along it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now there's people that live behind the Brinkleys, the Stevens?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Stevens, no they lived quite a way from the Brinkleys. They lived . . . they lived kind of down in the flat from the Dodgsons but their road came from the other side also.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So theirs came from the Hoovers and Coxes side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Hoovers and Coxes were down . . . way down it, but there was no road in there

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So how did the.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] He said they came in off the county road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Off the county road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [KEVIN] Probably out there by the Brinkleys.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Because they were practically behind Brinkleys.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was the Stevens?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. The Stevens family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And where did the Dodgsons live then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Dodgsons were right in . . . the area that I took you up there the time where all that poison oak was?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the Dodgson homestead.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that would be off the 00 road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then did anybody else live here besides the Stevens and the Dodgsons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The only family that lived in this area but would be that way more would be the Hoovers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, the Hoovers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And that was it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those houses were up on the other side of the valley there. So far as you know there were no houses on this side of the valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. And they were down in the flat like that. . . where that road that we started to come in, it veered to the left and there's quite a large flat area there where they farmed and the home was right in that flat area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hoovers was kind of up against this hill. The ridge, but the other house was down in the flat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then down in this area here, can you recall any orchards or any signs of Indian artifacts or any horses, old horses trails?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not a thing. This was . . . used to run stock in here, people that lived here, they let couple cows and horses for use around the farm, but that was it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about this creek down here, did that have a name too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they just called that just a wash.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a wash.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Because it dried up in the summer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So no names to the prairie or the meadows here, just the land owners?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok. Good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jim, when we were coming over, you were talking about the rumor of stage hold ups on Gold.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember the stories you heard or. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All I heard was there was supposed to have been treasure somewhere in the Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Peak area, that's all I know. Supposed to have been held up, the stage held up and then the gold was supposed to been buried somewhere in that area. That's all there is to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember who told you that story?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, old man Brinkley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Brinkley told you about the gold.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he told me about the gold hold up and he also mentioned about the possibility something on top of Forest Peak that nobody really knew about but there was something up there and it was probably the pits.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any other stories he might have told you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: APPENDIX

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Autobiographical Sketch

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following autobiographical sketch was written by James Hanish after reviewing the text of his oral history interviews.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Grandfather Hanish

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grandpa Hanish came from Austria with his parents when he was a small child. Later in life he met a girl who also came from Austria. They married and had two sons: Fred and Harry, and four daughters: Lora, Nora, Cora, Erma. Grandpa Hanish served in the civil war, and died in the Old Soldier House, Terra Haute, Indiana.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Mother's Family History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My mother's mother, Pearl Meador, was of New England stock. From what I heard, the early ancestors came over on the Mayflower and the ship made several trips from England. The Meador family settled in Battle Creek, Michigan. During that time Kellogg was starting to experiment with Corn Flakes. My grandmother, Pearl Meador, met Thomas O'Neil, her future husband and married him in Chicago. They had six children: Louie, Lint, Clara, Betty, Grace, Anna Marie. My grandfather O'Neil came from Toronto, Canada, year unknown.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Early Life of Father and Mother

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My father was 16 years old when his father told him, "I have too many mouths to feed, you will have to go on your own." Dad left Terra Haute and rode box cars to the western states, where he started his future work as a cloth cutter. He cut overalls in Tucson, Arizona, the moved to California. He returned east and then went to England, then to South America where he had a chance to work in Rio De Janeiro, but he didn't speak Spanish.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He returned to Chicago and started to work as a tailor, then became a clothing cutter. In those times men carried revolvers, as protection, and Dad kept his in his high pocket as he worked. The foreman tapped him on his shoulder and told him, "Check the gun, it's not allowed on the job." Dad's clothing cutting shears have been exhibited at the Homer Museum (Oregon State University.)

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dad roamed around Chicago a lot, and finally moved into a flat near where the O'Neil family lived. He and Lint O'Neil went around a lot together. Then he met Connie O'Neil, who was Lint's sister. After a courtship, they married. Mother was 15 and Dad was 30 years old. Her parents were not too happy about it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ma was 16 when I was born in the back of Dad's tailor shop. Ma told me about a lady friend her age who also had a baby. Ma and Grace Cushing used to race with their baby buggies down the sidewalk. It was a wonder both of us are alive today.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: My Life as a Boy

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I remember as a boy, about three or four years old, riding the El train going to the Circus on the lake front. Downtown was very crowded and windy, very hot in the summer, cold in the winter. Cobblestone streets, chain driven trucks and large horses pulling freight wagons, going on the steam boats. Sunday rides on Lake Michigan. My mother was living in Chicago when the tragic Eastland Excursion boat capsized; a great loss of life.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My Dad's brother Harry came to visit us. His family consists of his wife, Elizabeth, and son, Buddy. We never heard of them after the move to California.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Life in Elmhurst

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was two or three years old when we moved from Chicago to Elmhurst, Illinois. The town was 16 miles west of Chicago on the Chicago & Great Northwestern Railroad. I went to Kindergarten at the Eugene Field Elementary School.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I started to become interested in nature, as in rock formations, science, such things as star gazing, when I was 12 years old. My friends and I had similar interests in fishing, hiking, swimming, ice skating on frozen ponds. Never had any girl friends, too shy, darn it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My friend Clyde Swarnee and I used to ride freight trains. Our folks would drop dead if they knew of it.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Move to San Diego

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We left Elmhurst, Illinois, and moved to San Diego, California, where my Mother's family lived. My grandfather was foreman of the San Diego Tribune.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My folks rented an apartment in San Diego. Then they bought a lot in Chula Vista, a city in San Diego Bay, about 12 miles south of San Diego. I helped Dad build a stucco home, then a frame house later. In a few years he sold them and bought ten acres in Sunnyside, a small town 12 miles east of Chula Vista.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My work outside of home was ranch work, cement jobs, building foundations, even for a cemetery as gardener's helper. My hobbies were the same, looking for old mines, fishing, girl watching at the beaches.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Move to Oregon

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Depression really hit and we traded the ranch (10 acres) for 160 acres in Benton County, about twelve miles from Corvallis.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I returned to San Diego, California on my own and decided to work in Los Angeles, first at a cannery then the National Tank Manufacturing Co. on Santa Fe Avenue.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I returned to Oregon to the forty acres, due to severe depression in Steel work. My Dad was in Lakeview, Oregon working. I cut pulpwood. My Mother and I cared for the wood and garden raising.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Timber was all cut out of the 160 acres and we couldn't survive on the 40. Joe Smith foreclosed on the 40 and the 160 was turned back to the State. So my Dad and I worked on Lilly Lane in Corvallis for a lot to build a house. The house was built from lumber salvaged from the Berry Creek barn. I took harvest work or whatever I could find.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Return to California and Into the Service

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My uncle, Will Meador in El Cajon, California said his friend and partner was in the Naval Reserve, and was called in to assist the British to operate U.S. destroyers. His ship was the Reuben James. I helped my uncle to run his vegetable and fruit ranch: irrigate, train berry vines, drive a tractor. I made a soil conservation dam and I panned for gold in the creek but no luck.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I registered with the Selective Service Board in El Cajon. My uncle decided to sell the ranch. I went to San Diego to find work with an aircraft plant and was employed by Solar Aircraft, running power machines for parts for aircraft.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: After Pearl Harbor I enlisted in the Air Force. Basic training, schooling, then overseas: Scotland, England, France, Belgium, Germany.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Return to Corvallis

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then I came home to Corvallis, found work and met Grace R. Hartman. We married.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was employed at the Corvallis Lumber Company in Corvallis. Ben Greenwood was my foreman. Ted Huntly, supervisor. After a severe Union strike the mill closed down. Grace Hanish worked at J.C. Penney's Co. in Corvallis.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We decided to try Los Angeles for work. Grace Found work in the Broadway Department Store. We rented an apartment in Inglewood. Grace then worked in a dry cleaning plant, and I found work at Douglas Aircraft Plant, El Segundo.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: After various jobs and unemployment, Grace's son Ron wrote about a retirement home being built in Corvallis for which interviews were being done. Employment for 19 years. Then retirement, and shortly we moved to Cedar Crest. We were made managers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's my life and ours.
